If you don't impose the model with the types of training task you want them to excel at, they will not be good in, during test time. so specifically in the, in CLIP training, we are training images to be, image representations to be aligned with the captions representations, right? Usually, the caption focus more on the content of the, image, right? What's out there? What objects are there? What are they doing? But less, less on explicitly the positions of these, these objects, right?

If you have a human and dog on the image, the caption likely doesn't say like whether the human is on left, on the, on, on the right. It just say human plays with dog. That's kind of the natural thing we want to say when we see such an image. And that's, that's okay with, with human. We don't usually care about whether who's, who is on the left. But when we, i- we do-- If you want a model to be answering these type of questions well, then we need to use that in training, and that's what current CLIP training don't care about. so we end up with a CLIP model, that's going to be used as a vision encoder for multimodal language models, but it, it's not good at, it's not trained to be good at these spatial tasks or other types of, tasks that we, focus on in, in that, study.

So again, I think this just reinforce my idea that, if you want a model to be good at something, you need to train on that, that something. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: What are your thoughts about reinforcement learning? Do you think-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... um, like everyone, all the labs now are making their own versions of, uh, of environments, and they basically, "Yeah, we want to be good in coding. We want to be good in like some specific task, like make a specific environment. Let's train the model to be good on this, uh, environment. Give it feedback scores during these tasks, and that's it." Do you think this is the future? This is, we'll just see more and more environments like that?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah. actually, I don't know how feasible that is, given, like for every lab to really fine-tune these models using either reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning. I would, hope that, we have a common, we have a, we have a pipeline, a mature pipeline for, for the model to,... So this is closed source models that, that they give us like an interface to have a really strong general purpose model. I do hope that we, in the future, we have, another like tech- method that's as mature as pre-training for us to do continual training. and, it could be in refor- reinforcement learning. It also could be other more like context engineering, more, prompt engineering or agent collaborations.

I think all these are like, like open, and how maybe you, you, you, maybe you even need to tweak the architecture for, for the model to have large memory, larger context, things like that. Um- I do think the concept continual learning and adapting a general purpose do- to a particular domain is, is very important, because like each one throughout their life, they have different context. You want the model to be a good assistant to you to, to be able to empower your life, empower your work. You, you want a lot of conte-- you want a lot of context. And I think human brain still, is-- this is something the model hasn't been, able to match human brains, which is really a lot of memory and, and con-- and ability to learn fast, to remember fact just by seeing it once, and, and never forget. when, when my, when I interact with CloudCode today, the, the biggest thing I have to worry is, is whether it remember something I did before.

I think that, that's the experience of, a lot of people. and that's, that's kind of the-- in, in our professions, in our own particular career, we have a lot of things that we want the model to, to be able to remember so we don't have to repeat to it, to that, repeat on that. It's not necessarily, a particular task, but, just, just everything, like how our interaction with, with other people, history of, of, achievements, of, of failures, things like that. I think the answer to that may be more than just IL, on the right, on the data, but how the-- it's like a system engineering, how we, how we organize everything for the model to, to have easy access to. yeah, but it still falls onto the data, how we organize the data, how we feed enough data, how we, extract data from, from different sources, from different inputs.

Maybe we'll wear, wear glasses. We'll-- maybe we'll, wear these smart glasses so that we have, we have vision input to these models. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think like the basic components are there or like will stay the same? Do you think like we just need to build like the scaffolding, like, yeah, how to, I don't know, agent, agent move in the world or like something like that and collect data and bit organize it and memory and all these things? Or do you think we need to change something fundamentally?

Zhuang Liu: Yes. that's a very good question. I think the, the, I think, a sad fact is that, not, not, not everybody is able to work on the fundamental side on, on these very large models. people who can afford to train them can experiment with that. That's why we see a lot of agents work right now because people, they can-- they kind of-- it's kind of the only thing they could, they could do to improve on the system. Not-- I think agents are wonderful, but I feel, I feel every kind of system of agents I build, every scaffolding, for example, I try to build a, a scaffold that lets a CloudCode model to run for a long time.

But I, I believe after a few weeks or a few months, the model will develop the-- I'll find a simple, simpler solution. I'd say, for example, prompting or using some built-in, built-in commands or skills that can achieve the same thing, but with much less, overhead, without, without like a Python scaffolding or something, something like that. So I do think in, in-- that, that's kind of the, also the big lesson. We, we want to keep the system simple and, and just, let it decide a lot of things by itself. But yeah, the sad fact is that not everybody is, is able to make, make contributions to the evolving abilities of these, these underlying models.

So we can-- what we can do is to, to, to context engineering the agents. but, I, I'm not sure which... I, I do think fundamental abilities-wise, we, we can still, can still catch up so that we need-- So every task we care about right now, we care about at a certain performance level, we can do with less agents, less scaffolding, but, but, more relying on the model capabilities. I think we're still, we're still on that curve. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But why we actually like care, right? Because like, and then you, you also say, right, like to-- at the end, all the problems we can solve with, uh, agents today or like there are no like fundamental problems that we can't solve, right? So yeah, it may be that we can build, uh, or tune models to be more efficient or like to learn with less, um, number of examples. Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. I think, agents still make mistakes, right? the Cloud, Cloud, Agent, Code Agents. And, I think a lot of mistakes it had in, in, it, it had for me was not, not remembering something, that's obvious. That's, that should be kind of obvious. So I do think, in terms of memory con-- memory and context are, are the like most important aspects right, right now, especially memory. I mean, I mean, they are the two sides of the same coin, right? If you, when, if you-- even if you have, unlimited context, you, if you, like in theory, you can access everything you said with, you told the model, but if, if it forgets or get facts wrong, then it still, doesn't have good memory.

And also how, how can we make... So when CloudCode announced the one million token as a context window a few days ago, I think everybody was very cheerful of that fact, including me. it's very, it's very good. But still the, how can we have unlimited memory? Unlimited. And this is like the continual learning problem, right? How can we not forget? How can we not forget, forget? I think that's something, that's something more important than, and more, would be more fruitful if we have success than how, how to build collaborative agents. The fact that we need a lot of agents is exactly because not, not one agent cannot remember everything, so we need them agent to do separate tasks.

If, if one agent can remember everything, and when it does one task, it doesn't forget about the previous task, then, um- Everything could be built under one agent. Just they could, they could be s-- parallelized on the back end of the servers of the, of the company, but, but if they just one personal assistant to us, that would be still be, more convenient than, than cos-- orchestrating multiple agents. Yeah.

Allen Roush: So, um, uh, let's see. Uh, in that same, uh, paper, right, that I'd asked about before, right, like eyes wide shut, um, uh, you suggested, I think, mixing in vision and self-supervised features, uh, to improve grounding. Um, what do you think the most ideal vision encoder for a, uh, like multimodal language model looks like if you optimize like jointly for both like language alignment and, um, uh, uh, fine-grained like visual discrimination?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think that's exactly the, the solution I have in mind right now is just to do both, just to do,... try to build in the, the,... Yeah, I think those are the two dominant paradigms for vision pre-training right now. I would say, I would add, a, a lot of people are talking about world models right now, right? So I would add like world models, so adding a temporal dimension on that vision, vision part, that would be also be very helpful,.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: What is-- Uh, uh, let's talk maybe, let's talk a bit about world models. Uh, what is your definition for world models?

Zhuang Liu: Oh, world model to me is just, predict how the world works, right? Predicting how the world works, given, given your current condition. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Wh- what does it actually mean? So do you think, I don't know, for example, a, a few weeks ago, there was a Stefano Soato here, uh, that claimed, yeah, LLMs have world models. And, uh, before there was a Yann or like, uh, I don't know, uh, Randall was here and claimed, "No, we need to explicitly, uh, build the, uh, world models, like models, world models for, for, for our models, and currently LLMs don't have it." Uh, what is your opinion? Do you think we can define something that we can actually like say, "Okay, these models have world models and are world models, and like these ones don't have some, I don't know, internal state that they can represent the world?"

Zhuang Liu: Yep. I think LLM have world models in ter- in, in the language space. That's, that's, definitely true. and, and language is a higher abstraction space, in terms of the, our, how, all the perception signals we receive. it, it has a, a actually very good world model, I would say. I often discuss history with, with ChatGPT, and, a few days ago, I told it to make a, make like, given a-- so there's something happened in the history, right, of, of China, and I wanted-- I, I feel, I feel unfortunate for one party there. And I told the ChatGPT that, "Can you imagine hypothetical, hypothetical scenario where that, losing country or, or state actually, actually won the war, and then everything was changed?" And actually, it gave very reasonable responses.

Like not, it's nothing, like if you put together all the small events, everything makes sense. It's just very small, like probability shift, how, how people made decisions there. And everything, everything follows. it's like real history. Like it could very be real, very, have been the real history. So in that sense, I think no human, at least like no novelist, no, historian could be, may, may be able to at least like exceed that level of, of logical deduction in that, that series of, events. I think they, they do have a much very good world model, just in a high, very, very high abstraction model. So I guess, when we say doesn't have, we don't have a world model right now, it's in the, in the vision space, vision signal perception space.

We cannot fully recover, simulate the, the model in, in pixel space. That's also very true. So I think whether, we have the world model depends on what level of the world, of the world you want to model, right? If you consider all the, the higher level events of the world to be, to be a, self-containing world, yes, we do have a world, world model by language model. But if you consider every pixel, every raw signals, every physical signals, including like not, maybe not only vision, but also every substance in the world, like, like physical properties, all these things, yes, we don't, we don't have, that kind level of world, fine-grained world model, yet.

And I think the, the reason, underlying reason is still vision has a, is a much higher throughput data modality. We still don't have the compute to, to model that perfectly.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So do you think, do you think we actually need world model for, I don't know, ninety-nine percent of our tasks to solve like ninety-nine percent of the tasks that actually like we are, uh, interested in?

Zhuang Liu: I think for, for digital work, white collar work, we don't. a lot of things operate on the digital space. at most, I need a model to be able to read my computer screen, and computer screen can also be kind of, digitized or compressed. Or at most, it's usually just a ima- set of images, like real, real-time video flows. And that would be, um- Easier. So, so right now the bottleneck for me to interact with cloud code, it's often me having to screenshot my, my screen. And that shouldn't be-- that should be, I think that should be solvable because these models may have access to our computer screens in a safe manner very soon.

And we, I, I, I don't need to, share a lot of context like how do I set up something on a website? Those kind of things I still need to, kind of sometimes screenshot to the cloud code. Yeah, but for physical work like, construction, driving, physical activities, yes, I do think we need, we need a vision world model because, the feedback we've seen in that kind of work is so fine-grained, so detailed. Like also like hair cutting, right? which, which part of hair you want to cut more or less, like how the hairstyle. It, that, that one, is not possible by consulting a language model. You need to, you need to see in the model if you want the model to, to do this work, like also like some physical, like medical surgeries.

I do think, I do think we need vision world models, for, for those. It's, it's obviously not more than one percent of work. It's, maybe like seventy percent of the work. Yeah, I think, I do think for, for like more than half of work, we, we, we do need a vision world model for the model to be really good at it. Yeah.

Allen Roush: Um, and then, uh, um, you have this cool paper here too that I was really, uh, fascinated by because we-- I have a, a paper here at ICLR, uh, about anti-slop and removing, uh, what I guess you might call an idiosyncrasy in an LLM, right? Because your paper here, "Idiosyncrasy in Large Language Models Finds That Model-Specific Signatures, uh, Survive, uh, Rewriting, Translation, and Summarization,"  uh, in some, some ways. So like, what do you think those signatures are really measuring, right? Like, is it pre-training data-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm

Allen Roush: ... post-training style or like slop, like what we do in ours? Uh, decoding behavior, also something I look at a lot or something more structural or what, what's your thoughts?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah. so, so this paper is about, was about doing the same classification of, of data source, data origin, but on language model outputs. So given a t-piece of text of, um-- We want the, a separate neural network model to be able to tell which language model generated this text. And we found that, it can be very, very accurate, up to ninety-nine percent accuracy when, when there are five candidate models. and, back then it was also quite surprising to us. But, now I do think people accept more and more that there are clues in this text generated by language models and other common, folks who are not AI researchers can also tell, which model likely generated this text.

So it's not as surprising right now because like each, each company found their own strategy to maximize their user engagement, and it could be different, like the model could output different styles. In ChatGPT, you could also explicitly select a lot of different styles right now. now I think people are less surprised about this. But, but in terms of components, what contributes to this? Yes, I think, I do think the, each provider's own choice of style matters a lot. How, how, the system prompt, right? We don't have access to a sys prompt. Do they tell the model to be verbose or concise or have bullets or not? and also post-training. Different, different, companies use different post-training strategies. and the, the way they hire the, annotators, how to, how to rate each response would also be, have systematic differences.

Yeah, that's how they instruct these p- annotators to annotate, right? So they end up encouraging different behaviors and post-train-- and also then pre-training as well. Pre-training, each company has different sources of pre-training. some companies may want their model to be better at, coding, math, reasoning. Some models, might optimize for, general knowledge coverage. and we don't-- the, the sad fact is that we don't, we don't know how much difference there is, so we can only use, the outputs as a, as, the, approximation. So, so yeah, I think everything mattered, but I, I would think post-training and, how they, how the provider designed the system prompts, is causing the difference, likely. Yeah, the majority of the difference.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: What do you think about pre-training? Do you think this, uh, you know, separation between pre-training, mid-training, the post-training will, uh, continue? Is it important? Is something like kind of fundamental there, or do you think it's just a way that we, they converge to, to do our training?
reference:
Mm, got it. I think pre-training and mid-training shares more than they, than, with post-training. post-training is kind of making it-- the objective is, is, kind of the reward signal is kind of different because now it involves human ju-- sometimes involve human judgment, human preferences. I think that's the biggest difference. pre-training and mid-training are all just autoregression, right? Just on different styles of, of data and different context lengths. So I, I think that's, pre-training and mid-training is, could be, could be-- I think mid-training is a more recent concept, right? Just, like a few years ago, we only had pre-training and post-training, but now we have mid-training. Mid-training is maybe a, a temporary state because mid-training is for, really for extending context lengths, for bringing higher quality data.

That's model training focu- to focus on higher quality data so I think this may be the, I don't have inside information in these companies, but I think this may be compromises we need to make, because we don't have enough compute to always train on super long context. So always train on-- We don't have enough data to always train on higher quality data. so I think pre-training and mid-training are kind of like both pre-training, quote unquote. post-training is different because it involves actually human steering of the model behaviors. I think that would still continue. That would still, the d- the, the difference would, would not, disappear. But I, I would hope that we have another stage of continual, continual training customized for each indivi- each user.

That would be v- really nice, like customizing the preferences, the memory needed, the, the style of the user. Yeah.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think it's more a practical choice than a fundamental separation. Especially pre-training and mid-training, right? You can be using the same training objective, but changing what data you feed the model, the mixture of data, or the length of the context. So where exactly does pre-training end and mid-training begin? I don't think there's a very clear boundary there.

But the order does make sense. You first want the model to have broad knowledge, broad capabilities, and then you train it to be useful in the particular ways you care about. And with reinforcement learning, you have a different kind of signal. You let the model try something and give it feedback on whether it succeeds. That's different from just learning to predict the next token in a fixed dataset. So I wouldn't say all these stages are exactly the same, either.

Whether we will always organize training into these separate stages, I'm not sure. I could imagine that we alternate between them, that the model gets experience, learns from feedback, and also continues learning from new data. But you still need to solve the problem we discussed earlier: when it learns something new, how do you keep the things it already knows?

So for me, the more interesting question is how to make that learning continuous. After we deploy the model, can it keep improving from its interactions, remember the context, and adapt to a particular person or a particular job? I don't think the current names of the training stages are fundamental to that. Yeah.

sol.text:
Yeah, I don’t think the separation is fundamental. It’s more a practical recipe we converged to because the stages have different data and different optimization properties. Pre-training gives the model broad knowledge and basic capabilities from a huge amount of relatively cheap data. Mid-training changes the mixture—maybe longer context, more code, more domain-specific or higher-quality data—and post-training teaches the model how to interact with users, follow instructions, and optimize for preferences or verifiable rewards.

But these boundaries are already becoming blurry. Reinforcement learning can also teach new knowledge and capabilities, and pre-training data can include instruction-like or synthetic data. In the future, I would expect something more continuous, where the model keeps learning from new data, feedback, and its own interactions without forgetting what it learned before. So I think the stages will probably remain useful engineering concepts, but I don’t think intelligence fundamentally requires three separate phases. The more fundamental question is still: what experience do we give the model, and how do we let it learn from that experience efficiently without forgetting?

r004.rationale: It attributes the stages to different data and optimization properties, not to resource constraints.

r005.rationale: It says the boundaries may blur and does not predict that post-training will remain distinct from the other phases.

r006.rationale: It proposes continual learning from interactions but does not specify that it will be tailored to each individual user.

opus.text:
Yeah, that's a good question. so my, my view is that the separation is mostly, a practical, engineering, artifact rather than something fundamental. like if you think about it, it's all the same thing, right? It's, it's gradient descent on, on some data with some objective. And what really differs between these stages is the data — the quality of the data, the, the amount of it, and, and how much you can afford to curate it. Pre-training is where you have, trillions of tokens of, of kind of, whatever you can get from the internet, mid-training is where you have maybe, billions of, higher quality, more curated tokens, and post-training is where you have, like, much smaller amount of really, really carefully, produced data, either by humans or by, by other models or by, by verifiers in the RL case. So it's, it's essentially a curriculum, from abundant and noisy to scarce and clean. And the, the fact that we draw hard boundaries between them, I think that's just, that's just how the org charts and the, the compute budgets are, are structured. Like, you pre-train once and then you post-train many times, so it makes sense to, to have a checkpoint there and amortize that cost. That's, that's a very reasonable, engineering decision, but I don't think there's, like, a law of nature saying there must be exactly three stages.

And actually, I mean, the, the evidence for that is, is that the naming keeps changing, right? Like "mid-training" as a term, it didn't really exist, two years ago. People discovered that if you, if you anneal the learning rate at the end and, and feed high-quality data at that point, you get, you get big gains, and then suddenly we needed a word for it. so, so the taxonomy is kind of, following the empirical findings rather than, rather than the other way around. and I would, I would guess, we'll keep inventing new stages, or, or merging them. Some, some labs already, kind of blur the line, where the, where RL data or, or instruction-like data is mixed into, into the later part of pre-training. And I think that's, that's a natural direction.

but, but having said that, I do think there is, there is something, real underneath, which is that, the data you see later has, has more influence on the final model. That's, that's not just a convention, that's just how, how optimization works. so as long as that's true, the ordering of data matters, and, and then some, some notion of, of stages will, will persist, at least in, in how we talk about it. and the more interesting question to me is, does this whole picture survive if we, if we really solve continual learning? Because, going back to what I said earlier, if, if the model can, can keep learning from your interactions, then, then there's no "post" anymore, right? There's no final checkpoint that you, you ship and then freeze. the training just, just never ends, and, and the distinction between pre-training and post-training becomes kind of, meaningless, it's just, it's just what the model saw yesterday versus what it, it saw today. I think that would be the, the real, the real change. but we're, we're not there, so, so for now, yes, I, I think the three stages will, will stay with us for, for a while. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. It’s a good question. Yeah. So I, I, I wouldn’t say this three-stage thing is, is like a fundamental law of, of how you have to train a model. I think it’s more, more of a, a practical pipeline that, that the field has, has converged to, because it, it matches how we, how we actually have to spend compute, and, and how we iterate.

So at the, at the end of the day, it’s all just training, right? You’re, you’re updating the same parameters, on some data, with some objective. Pre-training, mid-training, post-training, these are, these are labels we put on, on different mixtures of data, and, and slightly different objectives, at different points. And, and I do think the, the underlying principle is still the same one I, I keep coming back to. If you want the model to be good at something, you, you better train it on that something.

Pre-training is still, is still the foundation. That’s, that’s where you, you try to cover as much as possible. Internet-scale data, next-token prediction, one, one epoch or, or around one epoch, like we, we talked about. You’re, you’re just trying to put the world’s knowledge into the, into the weights. And, and I don’t think that part goes away. Like, like even if we, we get much better at later stages, you still need that, that broad coverage. Otherwise the model just, just hasn’t seen the thing.

And then mid-training, post-training, these are, these are more about steering. Like, higher-quality data, long context, annealing, instruction following, preference data, reinforcement learning on, on specific environments. And, and that’s also why, why I said earlier that a lot of the, the style difference, the idiosyncrasy between models, I, I would attribute more to post-training and, and system prompts, than to, to the, the core architecture. Because that’s where you, you really shape the behavior.

But, but is the separation itself important, like, is it fundamental? I, I, I tend to think no. It’s, it’s convenient. Pre-training is extremely expensive, so you, you do it rarely. Post-training is cheaper, you can, you can iterate, you can try different recipes, different annotator instructions. Mid-training is kind of this, this in-between, like you, you start mixing in better data, longer sequences, towards the end. So, so as an engineering pipeline, it, it makes a lot of sense.

What I, what I actually hope, and I, I mentioned this earlier, is that we get a, a method for continual training that’s as mature as pre-training. Because, because the, the real thing we want is not three stages, it’s, it’s a model that can keep learning, keep, keep absorbing new context, new data, without, without forgetting. If we had that, these stages would, would just blur. You, you start general, and then you, you gradually mix in more of what you care about. That’s, that’s more natural. That’s also closer to, to how people learn.

So, so I think the, the staged pipeline will, will stay for a while, just because of cost, and because we, we don’t yet have that continual-learning recipe. But I, I wouldn’t treat pre-training, mid-training, post-training as, as three different scientific objects. It’s, it’s data, and, and when you show the data, and, and how you weight it. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think it's mostly a practical choice, driven by the constraints of compute and data. 

Right now, pre-training is the most scalable, stable way to absorb vast amounts of raw, internet-scale data. You want the model to see as much diverse knowledge and content as possible to build that fundamental representation. And then post-training—whether it's supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning—is where you shape that behavior, teach it to follow instructions, align it with user preferences, or elicit reasoning. Mid-training, or annealing, kind of emerged because people realized that gradually shifting the data distribution towards high-quality, domain-specific data before post-training gives a much better transition. 

So practically, this separation exists because high-quality annotated data or reward signals are scarce and expensive, while raw text and images are cheap and abundant. It's just very efficient from an engineering perspective to do it in stages.

Is it fundamental? I, I don't think it's fundamentally necessary. If you look at human learning, we don't have this rigid separation where we just "pre-train" for many years on raw observation without interaction and then suddenly switch to post-training. We learn continuously, getting feedback, interacting, and absorbing new information all at the same time. 

So ideally, if we can develop mature techniques for continual learning—where a model can learn from new experiences, remember everything, and not suffer from catastrophic forgetting—then these boundaries might naturally blur together into one continuous learning process. But given the current tools and infrastructure we have, I think this staged paradigm will stay with us for quite some time, just because it's so reliable and effective.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes post-training as the stage using supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning to shape behavior and align with user preferences, with annotated data and reward signals.

r003.rationale: It says the separation is not fundamentally necessary and that continual learning could blur the boundaries, implying mid-training may be temporary.

r004.rationale: It explicitly attributes the staged design to practical compute and data constraints, including scarce and expensive high-quality signals.

r005.rationale: It predicts the staged paradigm, including distinct post-training, will remain for quite some time because it is reliable and effective.

r006.rationale: It proposes continual learning from new experiences generally, but does not say that a future continual-training stage would be tailored to each individual user.

kimi.text:
Yeah, I, I think the separation is, is largely a practical thing rather than something fundamental. At the end of the day, it's all the same process, right? You have data, you compute a loss on the data, you do gradient updates. The difference between pre-training, mid-training, and post-training is really just what data you feed the model, and, and what objective you use. Pre-training is next-token prediction on internet-scale data. Mid-training is kind of a transition, right? More high-quality data, long context extension, annealing. And post-training is, instruction following, preference optimization, RL on verifiable tasks. But the underlying mechanism is, is the same. So going back to what we discussed earlier, if you want the model to be good at something, you train it on that something, and the different stages are just, different somethings, arranged in a sequence.

And I do think the boundaries are already blurring. Like, RL post-training compute is growing very fast. People do continual pre-training all the time. And also, I think the reason we even need post-training as a separate stage is that we don't have a mature way to do continual learning yet, right? If you just keep training the model on your own data naively, it forgets, it loses the general abilities. So the, the practical solution is you freeze the general foundation model, and then you adapt it in, in a separate stage. Once we have better continual learning, better memory, I think maybe this separation just, disappears. You would have one model that just keeps learning, keeps being updated on new data, new interactions, without forgetting.

That, that being said, I think the separation caught on because it's useful. It's a reasonable decomposition of the problem. You build this general foundation once, which is very expensive, and then many people can adapt it cheaply for, for behavior, for style, for, for their specific tasks. So even if it's not fundamental, I, I would expect it to stay for a while, at least until we, we really solve the continual learning problem. Yeah.

r001.rationale: Pre-training is explicitly described as next-token prediction, but mid-training is only described as a transition involving higher-quality data, context extension, and annealing; its autoregressive nature is not stated.

r002.rationale: Post-training is distinguished by preference optimization and RL, explicitly invoking preferences as part of its training signal.

r003.rationale: The response says the stage boundaries may disappear once continual learning improves, indicating that mid-training may be temporary rather than permanent.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute a separate mid-training stage to resource constraints.

r005.rationale: It predicts that the separation will remain useful and persist for a while, until continual learning is solved, which includes post-training remaining distinct from earlier stages.

r006.rationale: It proposes continual updating on new data and interactions, but does not clearly state that the future continual-training stage will be tailored to each individual user.

fable.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I think, so first I should say I'm not in industry right now, so I, I can only, kind of, speculate from what, what we can see from outside. but I, I don't think the separation is fundamental. I think it's, it's more of a, it's a practical convergence. It, it, to me it's mostly about data, again. Like, the three stages, they are really just three different, buckets of data with different, different quality and different, cost, right? Pre-training is the, the cheap, internet-scale, low curation data, and post-training is the very expensive, curated data, human annotated or, or verified by, by some reward, and mid-training is kind of this, in-between thing that people, invented later when they realize the, the base model needs, say, long context or more code before you, before you do the, expensive part.

And, and the reason we, we have this order, I think there are two reasons. One is just cost. Training from scratch is so expensive that you, you want to reuse the base model, and you want to only, spend the, expensive data, once, at the end. and the second is, the model remembers, remembers what it sees last, much better. When the learning rate is decayed, when the, high-quality data comes at the end, the model, the behavior of the model is mostly shaped by that. So, so in a way, the, the separation is kind of an engineering solution to the forgetting problem we, we talked about, right? We can't, keep the model learning, learning forever without forgetting, so we, freeze the, the, the general knowledge in one stage and then, carefully add the, the behaviors in another stage.

So already I think the, the boundaries are, are blurring. people put, instruction data into pre-training now. they, they put reasoning traces into, mid-training. I, I, I think the pipeline is, is really becoming a curriculum. It's, it's just, what data at what point of the, the training. And if you look at it that way, then the, the three names are, are not so, not so important. what is important is the, the ordering and the, the mixing ratio of the data. that, that I think is, is where a lot of the, secret sauce of each company is right now.

And, and then in the, in the ideal world, I would hope it, it becomes just one process. Like, the model is, is continually trained, it, it receives new data every day, and there is no, no, kind of, clear line between, "This is pre-training, now we, we stopped, now we do post-training." Because that, that clear line is exactly why the model has this cutoff, why it, why it doesn't remember what I did with it, last week. So, so I think the separation will stay for a while just because of, of compute and, of, of how mature the pre-training recipe is. It's, it's very mature, it's very stable, everybody knows how to do it. But, but I don't think it's fundamental, and, and if we, we solve continual learning, I, I think the, the distinction just, goes away. Yeah.
